articles.title: Telehealth-related education and training: a systematic review of recent developments since the COVID-19 pandemic.
articles.dek: A systematic review of 51 telehealth education programs developed since 2020 found expanding training initiatives, but most lack comprehensive coverage of competency domains and experiential learning.
summary: This systematic literature review identified telehealth-related training and education programs implemented between 2020 and 2024. The authors searched peer-reviewed literature and included 51 articles (of 7,547 identified) that described specific program content or learning objectives for any educational level or health professional. Most programs were implemented in the USA (82%) and targeted to undergraduate students (51%), with increasing publication over the study period.

Most courses were developed by universities (53%), often in collaboration with health services, with content applicable across multiple specialties. Nearly all programs (90%) included participant evaluation. Course content typically addressed basic telehealth knowledge and skills, patient safety, and ethics, with learning objectives frequently focused on technology and communication. However, only four programs included all six Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC) telehealth competency domains.

The authors concluded that while telehealth education has expanded since the COVID-19 pandemic onset, current curricula lack experiential learning and comprehensive coverage of domains including ethics, legal requirements, billing, physical examination techniques, patient education, and telehealth eligibility criteria. The review suggests that standardised training applicable across disciplines, supplemented with site or specialty-specific modules, could improve resource efficiency.
articles.why: This review documents the landscape of telehealth training development in response to pandemic-driven healthcare delivery changes. Understanding gaps in existing curricula—particularly in ethics, legal frameworks, and clinical skills—may inform discussions among medical educators, curriculum developers, and health systems about competency standards needed for competent telehealth practice across professions.

evidence.design: Systematic literature review with independent dual data extraction and quality assessment against SQUIRE 2.0 guidelines
evidence.limitations_and_uncertainty: The abstract does not specify the search strategy details, database(s) searched, or geographic limitations beyond noting that 82% of included programs were from the USA, which may reflect publication bias. No interrater reliability statistics or sensitivity analyses are mentioned. The quality assessment against SQUIRE 2.0 is noted but specific quality ratings are not reported. Conclusions about missing content (experiential learning, ethics, legal requirements) are derived from content analysis of published descriptions; actual curriculum comprehensiveness may differ.

articles.title: Safety and immunogenicity of the 24-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine in healthy Chinese adults: two single-center, randomized, double-blind Phase 1 and Phase 2 trials.
articles.dek: A 24-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine demonstrated favorable safety and robust immunogenicity against all 24 serotypes in Chinese adults aged 18 years and older in Phase 1/2 trials.
summary: Two single-center, randomized, double-blind Phase 1 and Phase 2 trials evaluated PCV24 in healthy Chinese adults aged ≥18 years. Phase 1 enrolled 240 participants randomized to low-dose PCV24, high-dose PCV24, PPSV23, or placebo. Phase 2 enrolled 992 participants randomized to three PCV24 formulations (varying dose and adjuvant content), PPSV23, or comparator groups.

Post-vaccination adverse reactions within 30 days were predominantly grade 1–2 severity, with rare grade 3 events occurring only in the 0–7 day window. No vaccine-related serious adverse events were reported over the 6-month follow-up period. Immunogenicity testing in Phase 2 demonstrated that the high-dose PCV24 group met non-inferiority criteria for IgG seroconversion against all 24 serotypes compared with PPSV23.

These findings suggest PCV24 offers an expanded serotype coverage with an acceptable tolerability profile in adults. The results support advancing to larger efficacy trials, though effectiveness in preventing pneumococcal disease and performance in specific risk populations remain to be established.
articles.why: Current pneumococcal vaccines cover limited serotypes; a 24-valent option could broaden protection if efficacy is confirmed. These phase data from a Chinese population are relevant to global vaccine development discussions and may inform regional immunization strategies pending larger trials. However, immunogenicity does not guarantee clinical efficacy.
articles.evidence: Design: Two randomized, double-blind, controlled phase trials. Sample sizes: 240 (Phase 1) and 992 (Phase 2) participants. Major limitations: single-center design; no efficacy data (immunogenicity surrogate only); no effect sizes, confidence intervals, or statistical comparisons provided in abstract; follow-up limited to 6 months for safety; generalizability to non-Chinese populations unclear; full safety and immunogenicity analyses not detailed.

articles.title: Evaluating a multi-vaccine respiratory immunization strategy involving SARS-CoV-2, pneumococcal, and influenza vaccines in adults: A randomized, open-label, multicenter, controlled, non-inferiority Phase IV trial in China.
articles.dek: A randomized Phase IV trial in China found that co-administering inactivated SARS-CoV-2, pneumococcal, and influenza vaccines together preserved immune responses and demonstrated acceptable safety in adults.
summary: This randomized, open-label, multicenter Phase IV trial enrolled 1,404 adults aged ≥18 years (with equal representation of adults aged 18–59 and ≥60 years) across China. Participants were assigned to three groups: co-administration of WIBP-CorV (inactivated SARS-CoV-2 vaccine) with PPV23 (23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine) on Day 0 followed by WIBP-CorV with IIV4 (quadrivalent inactivated influenza vaccine) on Day 28; WIBP-CorV alone on Days 0 and 28; or PPV23 on Day 0 followed by IIV4 on Day 28. The trial was designed as a non-inferiority comparison.

Co-administration preserved humoral immune responses across all vaccine platforms. Non-inferiority was demonstrated for SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing antibodies and pneumococcal serotype-specific IgG responses when co-administered vaccines were compared with separate administration. Seroconversion rates were non-inferior for all pneumococcal serotypes, though results were less consistent for SARS-CoV-2 (after the second dose) and influenza A(H1N1). Age-stratified findings showed age- and strain-specific variation requiring cautious interpretation.

The safety profile was acceptable, with only slightly elevated rates of mild, transient local reactions in the co-administration group and no vaccine-related serious adverse events reported. The authors conclude that co-administering these three vaccines is feasible while maintaining immunogenicity and safety in the populations studied, potentially streamlining adult respiratory immunization programs.
articles.why: Multi-vaccine co-administration strategies may improve immunization coverage and reduce clinical visit burden if immunogenicity is preserved. These results contribute evidence on whether simultaneous administration of SARS-CoV-2, pneumococcal, and influenza vaccines is immunologically compatible in adults. However, clinically meaningful non-inferiority thresholds and the clinical significance of less consistent seroconversion for certain strains require further discussion in the context of established immunization guidelines.
articles.evidence: Randomized, open-label, controlled, non-inferiority Phase IV trial. Sample size: 1,404 adults. Major limitations: open-label design (no blinding); trial conducted in China, limiting generalizability; age-stratified findings were inconsistent across pathogens and strains; specific immunogenicity thresholds for non-inferiority and actual effect sizes are not provided in the abstract; the full text was not reviewed to assess whether clinical outcomes or disease prevention were evaluated.

articles.title: Effectiveness of Quality Improvement Strategies in Preventing Healthcare-Associated Infections Among Neurosurgical Patients Admitted to Intensive Care Units: A Systematic Review.
articles.dek: A systematic review found that structured quality improvement interventions, particularly external ventricular drain care bundles, consistently reduce healthcare-associated infections in neurosurgical and neurological ICU patients.
summary: This systematic review searched five major databases from January 2010 to May 2026 and identified 17 primary studies from 14 countries evaluating quality improvement strategies for preventing healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) in neurosurgical or neurological ICU populations. The review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and assessed risk of bias using appropriate tools (ROBINS-I, Cochrane RoB 2, Newcastle-Ottawa Scale) stratified by study design. Three additional systematic reviews were retained for contextual interpretation but excluded from primary synthesis.

Structured QI interventions consistently reduced device-associated infection rates across studies. EVD-specific care bundles showed the strongest evidence, with EVD-related infection rates decreasing from 14.35 to 3.21 per 1,000 catheter-days following bundle implementation; one study reported 20 consecutive infection-free months. Other device-associated infection prevention bundles demonstrated clinically meaningful reductions: VAP rates decreased from 68.2 to 47.4 per 1,000 ventilator-days, CAUTI rates from 24.9 to 13.4 per 1,000 catheter-days, and CLABSI rates reached zero in one study with sustained monitoring.

The authors concluded that structured QI interventions—particularly EVD-specific care bundles, device-associated infection prevention protocols, and staff education programs with compliance monitoring—consistently reduce HAI incidence in neurosurgical and neurological ICU settings. Although the evidence base is predominantly non-randomized observational and quasi-experimental studies, findings were directionally consistent across diverse healthcare systems and institutional contexts.
articles.why: Neurosurgical ICU patients face elevated infection risk due to frequent invasive device use (external ventricular drains, central venous catheters, urinary catheters, mechanical ventilation) combined with impaired neurological status. This review synthesizes fragmented evidence on QI strategies in this vulnerable population and may inform institutional efforts to design and implement infection prevention protocols tailored to neurocritical care. The consistent reductions observed across different healthcare settings and countries suggest potential generalizability of evidence-based bundle approaches.
articles.evidence: The primary evidence synthesis included 17 randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies, and observational cohort studies. Three systematic reviews were retained for contextual interpretation but excluded from primary synthesis to avoid duplication. Risk of bias was predominantly low to moderate across included primary studies. Sample sizes of individual studies are not reported in this abstract. Major limitations include the predominantly non-randomized nature of the evidence base, and the abstract does not specify whether meta-analysis was performed or report statistical measures of heterogeneity, confidence intervals, or p-values for the reported infection rate reductions.

articles.title: Albuminuria as a Clinical Marker of Subclinical Myocardial Dysfunction in Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
articles.dek: In diabetic patients, urinary albumin excretion is associated with greater subclinical heart muscle dysfunction on echocardiography despite normal ejection fraction.
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether albuminuria (protein in urine) correlates with subclinical myocardial dysfunction in adults with diabetes. Researchers searched four electronic databases through March 2026 for observational studies comparing diabetic patients with and without albuminuria. Eighteen reports from 17 independent cohorts were identified; eight contributed data to quantitative pooling. The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale assessed study quality, and random-effects models combined results across echocardiographic measures.

Patients with diabetes and albuminuria had significantly lower global longitudinal strain (GLS) compared to those with normoalbuminuria (mean difference −1.38 percentage points; 95% CI −2.13 to −0.63; P < 0.001). Diastolic dysfunction markers (E/e') were also higher in the albuminuric group (mean difference 1.21; 95% CI 0.18–2.24; P = 0.021). Ejection fraction did not differ between groups. In multivariable analyses, albuminuria remained independently associated with impaired strain and approximately 5.5-fold higher odds of subclinical dysfunction.

The findings suggest albuminuria may serve as a clinical marker identifying diabetic patients with subclinical systolic and diastolic impairment despite preserved ejection fraction. The authors propose that urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio measurement could help flag asymptomatic individuals for consideration of deformation imaging (strain assessment), though they note prospective validation is needed before clinical implementation.
articles.why: Subclinical myocardial dysfunction in diabetes often progresses silently before overt heart failure emerges. If albuminuria reliably predicts early cardiac dysfunction, it could inform risk stratification conversations and guide decisions about cardiac surveillance intensity in asymptomatic diabetic patients. This may be particularly relevant when nephropathy is already documented.
articles.evidence: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (no randomized trials noted). Sample sizes for individual cohorts not reported in the abstract. Heterogeneity was substantial for GLS (I² = 82%), suggesting variability across studies. The abstract does not specify the total number of participants across all cohorts. Major limitations include the observational design (unable to establish causation), substantial statistical heterogeneity, and the requirement for prospective validation before clinical application. Certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE but specific grades are not detailed in the abstract.

articles.title: Berberine improves diabetic foot ulcer healing after tibial transverse osteotomy by inhibiting the PDGF-B/PDGFRβ signaling pathway.
articles.dek: A randomized controlled trial found that berberine injections added to tibial transverse osteotomy surgery improved diabetic foot ulcer healing rates and reduced markers of inflammation and fibroblast death.
summary: This was a prospective, single-center, randomized, placebo-controlled trial enrolling 96 diabetic foot ulcer patients (Wagner grade 2–4) scheduled for tibial transverse osteotomy. Participants were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive either local berberine injections or saline placebo as adjuncts to surgery. All 96 participants completed the 3-month follow-up with no dropouts. An additional 20 non-randomized participants (diabetic and healthy controls) were included for exploratory cellular studies only.

The berberine group achieved a higher total effective ulcer healing rate at 3 months (87.5% vs. 68.8%). Secondary improvements favoring berberine included greater increases in Ankle-Brachial Index (mean difference 0.13), faster ulcer area reduction (mean difference 16.7%), and greater reductions in inflammatory markers hs-CRP and IL-6. Exploratory findings showed berberine was associated with reduced fibroblast apoptosis in wound tissue and lower protein expression of PDGF-B and PDGFRβ. No serious adverse events attributable to berberine were reported.

The authors propose that berberine's effects may involve downregulation of the PDGF-B/PDGFRβ signaling pathway, which the authors suggest could reduce harmful fibroblast death and support wound healing. However, the authors explicitly note these associations are correlative and require further mechanistic validation. The study design does not establish causality for the proposed pathway.
articles.why: Diabetic foot ulcers remain a significant clinical challenge with high morbidity. This trial raises the question of whether adjunctive berberine—a natural compound with reported anti-inflammatory properties—might enhance surgical outcomes in a subset of patients. If confirmed in larger multi-center studies, such an approach could inform discussions about multimodal wound care strategies. However, the findings are limited to this specific surgical population and setting, and clinicians should await larger, independent validation before considering implementation.
articles.evidence: Randomized controlled trial with 96 participants in the active arms (berberine and placebo groups, n=48 each). No trial registration number, funding source, or blinding methods are described in the abstract. Major limitations include single-center design, lack of detail on allocation concealment and blinding procedures, small sample size, short follow-up duration (3 months), and exploratory rather than pre-specified biomarker analyses. The mechanistic pathway (PDGF-B/PDGFRβ) is inferred from secondary measurements, not directly tested. Generalizability to other surgical settings and patient populations is unclear.

articles.title: Gut virome remodeling after fecal microbiota transplantation is associated with virus-bacteria co-variation and metabolic response in obesity and type 2 diabetes.
articles.dek: Viral community changes in the gut after fecal microbiota transplantation tracked alongside bacterial shifts and showed comparable predictive accuracy for metabolic response in obesity and type 2 diabetes.
summary: This was a randomized controlled trial examining longitudinal fecal samples from participants with obesity and type 2 diabetes who received fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) alone, FMT with lifestyle intervention, or sham procedure with lifestyle intervention. Researchers used specialized sequencing to characterize both viruses and bacteria in the gut microbiota.

Post-FMT virome changes distinguished LDL responders from non-responders with 84.8% accuracy, comparable to bacterial changes (81.4%). Donor-derived viral sequences were detected in 64.7% of FMT-alone recipients and 58.8% of FMT-plus-lifestyle recipients, versus 5.6% in the sham group. FMT was associated with increased viral diversity, shifts toward donor viral communities, and coordinated virus-bacteria associations. Most responsive viruses were Caudoviricetes that were predicted to infect bacteria including Roseburia, Bifidobacterium, Escherichia, Blautia, and Enterococcus.

The findings suggest that the gut virome—not just bacterial composition—represents an important ecological component linked to FMT outcomes and metabolic improvements in obesity and type 2 diabetes, though the specific mechanisms driving clinical benefit require further investigation.
articles.why: Viral communities have been largely overlooked in FMT research, which has traditionally focused on bacterial engraftment. This work raises the possibility that characterizing viral-bacterial interactions alongside traditional microbiome analysis could help predict which patients will respond metabolically to FMT and potentially improve patient selection or monitoring strategies. Understanding virus-bacteria ecology may also inform future microbiota-based interventions.

evidence.design: Randomized controlled trial with longitudinal fecal sampling and virus-like particle-enriched metagenomic sequencing combined with bulk-DNA metagenomic sequencing.
evidence.sample_size: FMT alone (n=17), FMT with lifestyle intervention (n=17), sham with lifestyle intervention (n=18); total sample size across trial groups reported but specific demographic details not provided in abstract.
evidence.major_limitations: Abstract does not specify: baseline characteristics or demographic composition; timing of follow-up assessments; whether metabolic outcomes (e.g., LDL changes) were primary or secondary; full clinical criteria for 'responders' versus 'non-responders'; mechanistic confirmation of virus-bacteria associations beyond computational prediction; generalizability to other populations; trial registration number or publication date. The predictive accuracy metrics require consideration of model validation methods not detailed here.

articles.title: From Bench to Bedside: Evaluating the Accuracy of Clinical Sensory Testing in Detecting Somatosensory Disorders. A Systematic Review.
articles.dek: A systematic review of 12 studies (N=4,911) found that clinical sensory tests show moderate to high specificity for detecting somatosensory disorders, but sensitivity varies widely and methodological heterogeneity limits their use as standalone diagnostic tools.
summary: This systematic review searched five databases (Medline, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, EMBASE, Scopus) through August 2025 for studies evaluating clinical sensory testing (CST) accuracy in patients with somatosensory dysfunction, comparing CSTs against reference standards. Twelve studies were included covering conditions such as diabetic peripheral neuropathy, lumbar spinal stenosis, and neuropathic pain. Two independent reviewers assessed study quality using QUADAS-2 and performed narrative synthesis organized by sensory modality.

Results showed that CSTs demonstrated moderate to high specificity overall, particularly for pressure, mechanical, and vibration testing. The Semmes-Weinstein Monofilament Test reported 77%–90.7% sensitivity and 63.8%–100% specificity; tuning fork vibration tests ranged from 30%–96% sensitivity and 45%–99% specificity. Thermal testing exhibited the greatest accuracy variability (sensitivity 0.0%–97.1%; specificity 2.0%–94.4%). Composite (multimodal) testing tools yielded higher accuracy, often exceeding 87% for both sensitivity and specificity.

The authors conclude that CSTs are pragmatic for preliminary somatosensory assessment, especially when using multiple modalities together, but cannot reliably serve as standalone diagnostic tests due to wide sensitivity-specificity intervals and substantial methodological heterogeneity across studies. High or unclear risk of bias was present in the majority of included studies. The review emphasizes that protocol standardization and validation against robust reference standards are needed before CSTs can be reliably integrated into routine clinical diagnostic practice.
articles.why: Clinical sensory testing is widely used in patient evaluation for conditions affecting sensation (neuropathy, spinal stenosis, neuropathic pain). This review clarifies that while these tests have reasonable specificity—making them useful for ruling-in disorders in certain contexts—their variable sensitivity means they should not be used in isolation for diagnosis. The findings may inform clinical teams about the importance of multimodal testing approaches and the need for clinical correlation rather than reliance on single sensory measures. This could support more thoughtful test selection and interpretation in routine practice.

evidence.design: Systematic review of studies comparing clinical sensory tests to reference standards; narrative synthesis organized by sensory modality
evidence.sample_size: 12 included studies with total N=4,911 participants
evidence.conditions_evaluated: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy, lumbar spinal stenosis, neuropathic pain, and other somatosensory disorders
major_limitations: High or unclear risk of bias in at least one QUADAS-2 domain for the majority of included studies
Substantial methodological heterogeneity across studies limits direct comparison
Wide and overlapping sensitivity-specificity ranges across different tests and modalities
Thermal testing showed particularly high accuracy variability (0%–97.1% sensitivity), suggesting inconsistent methodology or clinical application
Full-text article not reviewed; information limited to abstract and structured data
evidence.missing_information: Specific risk of bias patterns, meta-analysis results (if conducted), trial registration details, publication date of this review, and confidence intervals for reported ranges

articles.title: A Systematic Review of Complications Following Elective Foot and Ankle Surgery.
articles.dek: A systematic review of nine studies found that complications after elective foot and ankle surgery occur at variable rates, with infection, wound problems, nonunion, and nerve injury among the most common, and diabetes, obesity, smoking, and vascular disease as consistent risk factors.
summary: This systematic review searched PubMed, Scopus, and CINAHL for studies published between January 2020 and June 2025 reporting postoperative complications in adults undergoing elective foot and ankle surgery. Nine studies encompassing 20,455 patients were included. Data on complication types, incidence rates, and risk factors were extracted and synthesized narratively because study heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis.

Complication incidence varied substantially across studies: infection ranged from 0.3% to 12.5%; wound healing problems from 0.5% to 10.0%; nonunion from 0.8% to 18.7%; hardware removal from 3.8% to 15.5%; nerve injury from 0.2% to 10.0%; pain or stiffness from 0.8% to 18.7%; and systemic complications from 3.6% to 7.4%. Diabetes, obesity, smoking, and peripheral vascular disease were identified as consistent risk factors across procedures. Higher complication rates were associated with revision surgery, prolonged operative time, and multisegment reconstruction.

The authors conclude that postoperative complications following elective foot and ankle surgery are common and multifactorial, with identifiable risk patterns that are consistent across different procedures. They suggest this evidence supports improved preoperative risk stratification, targeted preoperative optimization strategies, and structured postoperative care protocols.
articles.why: This review provides a broad overview of complication profiles across elective foot and ankle procedures rather than single-procedure analyses, potentially helping clinicians appreciate the range and frequency of postoperative problems. Identification of modifiable risk factors (smoking, obesity) and patient characteristics (diabetes, vascular disease) may inform preoperative counseling and candidate selection. The finding that operative factors such as prolonged surgery time and revision status associate with higher complication rates could prompt discussion of procedural planning and complexity, though the review does not establish causation.
articles.evidence: Systematic review synthesizing nine observational studies totaling 20,455 patients. No randomized trials are indicated. Major limitations include substantial heterogeneity in study designs, populations, outcome definitions, and measurement periods, which precluded quantitative synthesis. The abstract does not specify individual study quality assessment methods, follow-up duration, or consistency of complication definitions across studies. Variation in reported complication rates is wide, suggesting differences in case mix, surgical technique, or ascertainment. The review identifies associations with risk factors but cannot establish causality.
articles.journal: Journal of foot and ankle research

articles.title: Chios Mastic in Well-Controlled Hypertension: Findings From the HYPER-MASTIC Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.dek: A 3-month randomized trial found that Chios mastic supplementation did not reduce blood pressure in adults with well-controlled hypertension, though transcriptomic changes suggest potential vascular effects in higher-risk subgroups.
summary: This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 106 adults with stable, well-controlled hypertension and variable cardiovascular risk. Participants received low-dose Chios mastic (1500 mg/day), high-dose Chios mastic (2800 mg/day), or placebo for 3 months. The primary outcomes were changes in 24-hour ambulatory systolic and diastolic blood pressure; secondary outcomes included vascular function markers, oxidative stress, proteasome activity, and transcriptomic profiling in a high-risk subgroup.

No significant between-group differences were observed in 24-hour systolic or diastolic blood pressure. Oxidative stress markers and proteasome activity showed no changes across groups. However, in participants identified as higher-risk, mastic supplementation induced distinct transcriptomic changes, particularly in pathways related to endothelial junction organization and vascular integrity. The intervention was well tolerated with high adherence, confirmed by dose-dependent increases in mastic-derived plasma compounds.

The authors interpret the null blood pressure findings as reflecting a ceiling effect—participants already had well-controlled hypertension and low baseline cardiovascular risk, potentially limiting room for further reduction. The transcriptomic signals in higher-risk individuals suggest biologically meaningful vascular effects may exist but were not captured by the study's primary hemodynamic measures or other inflammatory and oxidative stress markers.
articles.why: This trial addresses whether natural compounds can provide incremental cardiovascular benefit in the common clinical scenario of patients on antihypertensive therapy with controlled blood pressure but residual vascular risk. The negative primary result in low-risk, well-controlled patients suggests Chios mastic is unlikely to offer additional blood pressure-lowering benefit in this population. However, the distinct transcriptomic findings in higher-risk participants raise questions about whether such supplementation might merit investigation in less-controlled or higher-risk populations, and whether gene expression changes correlate with clinically meaningful outcomes.

major_limitations: No significant blood pressure reduction observed; unclear whether null finding reflects true inefficacy or insufficient study power and duration
Oxidative stress and proteasome activity markers did not change, limiting understanding of proposed mechanisms
Transcriptomic findings are from a predefined high-risk subgroup only; sample size for this analysis not specified
No functional validation that transcriptomic changes translate to clinical benefit
Follow-up duration (3 months) may be insufficient to detect long-term vascular effects
Full publication date and trial registration number not provided in abstract
